# How to use this guide

Industrial Pharmacy II is a descriptive subject about how a product moves from the laboratory to the market: scale-up, technology transfer, regulatory approval and quality systems. There are very few numbers to learn, so marks come from clear definitions, well-ordered lists, flow charts of procedures and tables comparing agencies or guidelines. Study one unit a day. Read the notes, close them, and write each flow chart (pilot plant set-up, TT process, drug development path, OOS investigation, change control, QbD steps, Indian new drug approval) from memory. Finish with the question bank and the MCQs for that unit.

The notes follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 3 is the largest and is split into Part A (regulatory affairs as a function) and Part B (requirements for drug approval: non-clinical studies, IND, IB, NDA, clinical and BE studies, protocols, biostatistics, data presentation and trial management). No unit has been merged or moved.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long (10-mark), short (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions. The very short ones are good warm-ups and help with MCQs.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a flow chart or table.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Pilot plant scale-up | Objectives and general considerations (personnel, space, raw materials), scale-up of tablets, liquid orals and semisolids, SUPAC (types and levels of change), platform technology |
| 2 Technology transfer | WHO TT guideline terms, TT protocol, transfer from R&D to production, granularity, analytical method transfer, Indian TT agencies (NRDC, TIFAC, BCIL, APCTD, TBSE/SIDBI), confidentiality agreements, MoU, licensing |
| 3 Regulatory affairs and drug approval | Role and responsibilities of RA, history of drug laws, IND types and contents, Investigator's Brochure, NDA, phases of clinical trials, BE studies, clinical protocol, biostatistics terms |
| 4 Quality management systems | TQM, QbD elements, Six Sigma and DMAIC, OOS investigation, change control, ISO 9000 family, ISO 14000, NABL, GLP |
| 5 Indian regulatory requirements | Organisation and functions of CDSCO and State Licensing Authority, CTD modules, COPP, approval procedure for new drugs |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Start every answer with a one-line definition, then go to a numbered list. Expand every abbreviation the first time you use it (TT, QbD, OOS, CTD, COPP, IND, NDA, SUPAC, NABL, GLP).
2. Draw a flow chart for every procedure: TT steps, drug development, OOS investigation, change control, PDCA, DMAIC, QbD, new drug approval in India. A neat chart earns a large share of the marks.
3. Use tables for comparisons: QA vs QC, certification vs accreditation, ISO 9001 vs GMP, IND vs NDA vs ANDA, CDSCO vs State Licensing Authority, SUPAC levels, the five CTD modules.
4. Learn the small set of fixed facts exactly: SUPAC Levels 1–3, f2 50–100, BE 90% CI 80–125%, Six Sigma 3.4 DPMO, ISO 9001 / 14001 / 17025 / 15189, CTD five modules, IND 30-day wait, NDCT Rules 2019 and the main CT forms.
5. For regulatory questions, name the authority and the law (for example "CDSCO under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and NDCT Rules 2019"). Rules change, so in real work always check the current text on the official website.
6. In "write a note on" questions about an agency (NRDC, TIFAC, NABL), give full form, parent body, role and one example of its work.
7. End long answers with advantages or significance; examiners in this subject reward a closing point.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, prepare these with a flow chart or table each: **pilot plant general considerations and SUPAC**, **technology transfer protocol and steps**, **IND, IB and NDA**, **QbD**, **OOS investigation and change control**, and **CDSCO / State Licensing Authority with the new drug approval procedure**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Unit 1 — Pilot plant scale-up**

- Pilot plant = lab formula → reliable, economical process on production-like equipment. Pilot batch (solid orals) ≥ 10% of production or 100,000 units, whichever is larger.
- General considerations: reporting responsibility, personnel, space (administration, physical testing, equipment floor, storage), formula review, raw materials, equipment, production rate, process evaluation, master manufacturing procedures, stability, GMP.
- Solids: blending, granulation end point, drying, milling, lubrication time, compression speed. Liquids: agitation, heating/cooling, filtration, homogenisation. Semisolids: heating/cooling rates, shear, vacuum mixing.
- SUPAC (US FDA): IR, MR, SS; changes in components, site, batch size, equipment, process. Level 1 annual report; Level 2 supplement; Level 3 prior approval. Batch size up to 10× = Level 1. f2 50–100 = similar.
- Platform technology: reusable system (OROS, HPMC matrix, liposomes, hot-melt extrusion, mAb and mRNA platforms).

**Unit 2 — Technology transfer**

| Item | Key facts |
| --- | --- |
| WHO guideline | TRS 961, Annex 7 (2011) |
| Terms | Sending unit, receiving unit, protocol, report, gap analysis, CQA, CPP, design space |
| Steps | Team → gap analysis + risk → protocol → documents + training → method transfer → trial and validation batches → report → filing |
| Granularity | API, excipients, finished product, packaging |
| Method transfer | Comparative testing, co-validation, revalidation, waiver |
| Agencies | APCTD/APCTT (UN-ESCAP), NRDC (1953, DSIR), TIFAC (1988, DST), BCIL (DBT), TBSE/SIDBI |
| Documents | Confidentiality agreement, MoU, licensing agreement (exclusive/non-exclusive, royalty), quality agreement |

**Unit 3 — Regulatory affairs and drug approval**

- RA roles: strategy, dossier, submission, labelling, life cycle, compliance, intelligence.
- History: 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act; 1938 FD&C Act (sulfanilamide elixir); 1962 Kefauver–Harris (thalidomide; efficacy); 1984 Hatch–Waxman (ANDA); 1990 ICH.
- Non-clinical: pharmacology + safety pharmacology core battery; ADME + toxicokinetics; toxicity (acute, repeated dose, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive, local).
- IND: 21 CFR 312, Form 1571 (sponsor), 1572 (investigator); types investigator, emergency, treatment, commercial; start after 30 days if no clinical hold.
- IB: clinical + non-clinical data for investigators (ICH E6); updated yearly.
- NDA: 21 CFR 314, Form 356h; 505(b)(1), 505(b)(2), 505(j) ANDA; BLA for biologics.
- Phases 0–IV. BE: crossover, washout, Cmax, AUC; 90% CI 80–125%.
- Biostatistics: α 0.05, power 80–90%, p-value, CI, t-test, ANOVA. Submissions: eCTD, ICH E3, CDISC (SDTM, ADaM).

**Unit 4 — Quality management systems**

- QM ⊃ QA ⊃ GMP ⊃ QC. Juran: fitness for use; Crosby: conformance to requirements.
- TQM: customer focus, all employees, process approach, continual improvement, PDCA; seven tools (fishbone, Pareto, control chart …).
- QbD (ICH Q8(R2)): QTPP → CQA → risk assessment (Q9) → DoE → design space → control strategy → life cycle; Q10 quality system; PAT.
- Six Sigma: 3.4 DPMO; DMAIC; DMADV; belts; Cpk ≥ 1.33.
- OOS: Phase I lab → Phase II full investigation → CAPA; no testing into compliance.
- Change control: request → classify → impact → approve → implement → notify → verify → close.
- ISO 9000 vocabulary; 9001 requirements (certifiable); 9004; 19011 auditing; 7 principles. ISO 14001 = EMS.
- NABL (QCI): ISO/IEC 17025 labs, ISO 15189 medical labs. GLP: OECD principles, 21 CFR 58 (1978), NGCMA (DST); study director + QA unit.

**Unit 5 — Indian regulatory requirements**

| Topic | Key facts |
| --- | --- |
| CDSCO | NRA under DGHS, MoHFW; DCGI heads; zonal, sub-zonal, port offices; central labs; DTAB, DCC; SECs |
| CDSCO functions | New drugs, clinical trials, imports, standards, EC registration, joint licensing (vaccines, LVPs, blood products, r-DNA), devices, COPP |
| State Licensing Authority | Manufacturing and sale licences, inspection, sampling, prosecution, recall |
| CTD (ICH M4) | M1 regional; M2 summaries; M3 quality; M4 non-clinical; M5 clinical |
| COPP | WHO certification scheme format; CDSCO issues after WHO-GMP compliance |
| New drug | NDCT Rules 2019; CT-04 → CT-06 (trial); CT-18 import, CT-21 manufacture; 90 working days (30 for India-developed, deemed approval) |
| Post-approval | PSUR 6-monthly for 2 years, then yearly for 2 years; Phase IV if required |

questions.answer:
1. Pilot plant: part of the industry where a laboratory formula is turned into a viable product by developing a reliable, practical and economical procedure on equipment similar to production machines. Scale-up: increasing batch size (lab → pilot → production) while keeping quality the same.
2. Objectives: try the process on production-type equipment; find critical variables and set limits; make batches for clinical, stability and regulatory use; write master manufacturing procedures; test commercial raw materials; train staff; estimate cost and yield.
3. Reporting responsibility: works between R&D and production with QA, QC, engineering and regulatory affairs.
4. Personnel: knowledge of pharmaceutics, chemistry and engineering, hands-on experience with machines, communication and report writing, GMP and validation knowledge.
5. Space: administration and information processing; physical testing area; standard equipment floor with utilities; storage areas for approved, quarantined, in-process and finished material.
6. Review of formula: reason, grade, supplier and quantity of each ingredient, order of addition.
7. Raw materials: test lots from commercial suppliers; particle size, density, moisture and polymorphic form may differ from lab lots; set specifications and qualify suppliers.
8. Equipment: economical, easy to clean, same principle as production.
9. Production rate: decided by market demand.
10. Process evaluation: order and time of mixing, rate of addition of fluids, heating/cooling rates, screen and filter size, drying temperature and time.
11. Master manufacturing procedures, stability and uniformity of pilot batches, and GMP (qualification, validation, cleaning, documentation).
12. Significance: prevents costly production failures and gives data for validation and regulatory filing.
questions.question: Define pilot plant and scale-up. Discuss the objectives and general considerations (personnel, space, raw materials and other requirements) of a pilot plant.

questions.answer:
1. Material handling: manual at lab scale, bins and vacuum/gravity transfer at large scale; watch dust and segregation.
2. Dry blending: blender type, fill volume, speed and time; blend uniformity with sampling thief; over-mixing can demix.
3. Wet granulation: high-shear mixer impeller and chopper speed, amount and rate of fluid, end point by power consumption or torque. Dry granulation: roll pressure and gap.
4. Drying: tray vs fluid bed dryer; inlet temperature, airflow, load, time; loss on drying end point.
5. Milling: mill type, screen size and speed decide granule size distribution, flow and weight variation.
6. Lubrication: magnesium stearate mixing time is critical; over-mixing lowers hardness and slows dissolution.
7. Compression: high-speed rotary press with short dwell time, forced feeders, tooling, precompression; capping and sticking may appear only at speed.
8. Coating: pan size and speed, spray rate, atomising air, inlet temperature, number of guns, load.
9. Capsule filling: from hand filling to dosator or tamping machines; powder flow and plug formation must suit the machine.
10. Documentation: master formula record, batch manufacturing records, scale-up/development report, specifications for raw materials, in-process and finished product, SOPs for equipment, process validation protocol and report, stability protocol and data, change control records.
11. Conclude with a flow chart: weigh → mix → granulate → dry → mill → lubricate → compress → coat, showing the parameter checked at each step.
questions.question: Discuss the pilot plant scale-up considerations for solid dosage forms (tablets and capsules). Add a note on relevant documentation.

questions.answer:
1. SUPAC = Scale-Up and Post-Approval Changes; US FDA guidance on what tests and filings are needed when an approved product is changed, so that quality and performance stay the same.
2. Family: SUPAC-IR (immediate-release solid orals), SUPAC-MR (modified-release solid orals), SUPAC-SS (non-sterile semisolids); plus an equipment addendum classifying equipment by design and operating principle.
3. Types of change: components and composition; site of manufacture; batch size (scale-up/down); manufacturing equipment; manufacturing process.
4. Level 1: unlikely to affect quality or performance; reported in the annual report. Example: batch size up to 10× the pilot/bio-batch with equipment of the same design; small excipient change within set limits; site move within the same facility.
5. Level 2: could have a significant effect; filed as a supplement. Example: batch size beyond 10×; equipment of different design and principle; larger excipient change; site within the same campus.
6. Level 3: likely significant effect; prior approval supplement. Example: site to a different campus; large excipient change or change in excipient type.
7. Tests: stability (accelerated and long-term data), dissolution profile comparison (single point or multipoint in one or several media), f2 similarity factor 50–100 for similarity, in vivo bioequivalence for some Level 3 changes; depth depends on level and BCS class.
8. Indian manufacturers follow SUPAC for US-market products; for India, post-approval changes follow CDSCO rules.
questions.question: What is SUPAC? Explain the types and levels of changes covered by SUPAC guidelines and the tests required.

questions.answer:
1. Administration and information processing area: offices, records, data handling, report writing.
2. Physical testing area: in-process and finished-product tests (hardness, friability, viscosity, particle size, moisture).
3. Standard pilot-plant equipment floor: production-type machines (mixers, granulators, dryers, presses, coaters, liquid tanks) with room to clean, move and change equipment; utilities such as purified water, compressed air, steam, dust extraction and HVAC.
4. Storage area: separate, labelled zones for approved raw materials, quarantined material, in-process material and finished pilot batches, with controlled temperature and humidity where needed.
5. Space should be flexible and GMP-compliant so new trials can be set up quickly.
questions.question: Write a note on space requirements of a pilot plant.

questions.answer:
1. Equipment: jacketed stainless-steel tanks, suitable agitators, homogenisers or colloid mills, filters, pumps, filling machines.
2. Mixing: agitator type, speed and position change with tank size; complete dissolution or wetting without trapping air.
3. Order of addition and temperature: e.g. sugar dissolved hot, preservative added at the correct temperature, flavour added after cooling.
4. Heating and cooling take longer in large tanks; risk of degradation and microbial growth.
5. Filtration: filter area and type, pressure, clarity; filter must not adsorb preservative.
6. Suspensions: particle size, wetting, viscosity, sedimentation volume, redispersibility; emulsions: phase temperatures, rate of addition, homogenisation pressure, globule size.
7. Checks: appearance, pH, viscosity, specific gravity, taste, microbial limits, preservative efficacy, fill volume and foaming.
questions.question: Discuss scale-up considerations for liquid oral dosage forms.

questions.answer:
1. Mixing vessels: jacketed, with anchor/scraper agitator plus high-shear homogeniser; vacuum to avoid air.
2. Heating and cooling rates: melting of fatty phase, temperature at which phases are mixed and cooling rate decide consistency and crystal formation.
3. Shear and mixing time: too much may break gel structure; too little gives lumps and uneven drug content.
4. Drug incorporation: dissolved or dispersed; control particle size by milling or levigation.
5. Transfer: suitable pumps and pipes for viscous mass; avoid air pockets.
6. Filling into tubes or jars at a suitable temperature.
7. Tests: appearance, homogeneity, viscosity/rheology, spreadability, pH, content uniformity and stability under heat and cold.
questions.question: Write the scale-up considerations for semisolid dosage forms.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a proven, reusable delivery or manufacturing system that can be applied to many drugs with only small changes.
2. Examples: osmotic pump (OROS-type) tablets; HPMC matrix tablets; liposomes and nanoparticles; hot-melt extrusion solid dispersions; orally disintegrating tablet technologies; prefilled syringes and inhalers; monoclonal antibody manufacturing platform; mRNA vaccine platform.
3. Advantages: shorter development time and cost; reuse of knowledge, equipment and validated processes; lower risk; easier regulatory review and technology transfer.
4. Limitations: not every drug suits the platform; patents may restrict use; each product still needs its own quality, safety and efficacy data.
questions.question: What is platform technology? Give examples, advantages and limitations.

questions.answer:
1. Process parameters: order of mixing; mixing speed and time; rate of addition of granulating fluid, solvent or drug solution; heating and cooling rates; screen and filter size; drying temperature and time.
2. Master manufacturing procedure: product name, strength, batch size; weighing sheet with each ingredient, quantity and lot number; equipment and settings; step-by-step processing directions; in-process checks with limits; sampling instructions; yield limits; signatures of operator and checker.
3. These documents ensure the process is repeatable at production scale.

questions.answer: Scale-up is increasing the batch size from laboratory to pilot to production while keeping product quality the same. Scale-down is decreasing the batch size, for example for a small market or to study a production problem.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a logical procedure that controls the transfer of a process, its documents and expertise between development and manufacture or between sites. WHO guideline: TRS 961, Annex 7 (2011).
2. Terms: sending unit (SU), receiving unit (RU), TT team, protocol, report, gap analysis, CQA, CPP, design space, acceptance criteria, QRM, commissioning.
3. Principles: planned and approved; RU capable; acceptance criteria agreed in advance; differences assessed for risk; transfer complete only when RU proves it meets specifications.
4. Steps: form team → gap analysis and risk assessment → approve protocol → transfer documents and knowledge → train RU staff → transfer analytical methods → trial batches → validation batches → stability → TT report → regulatory filing → routine production.
5. Process transfer: development report, master formula, critical parameters with ranges, in-process controls, batch records, stability, known problems.
6. Packaging transfer: specifications of primary and secondary packaging, compatibility and stability in the pack, special needs (desiccant, light protection).
7. Cleaning transfer: solubility, toxicity, potency for residue limits, cleaning agents and procedures, residue test methods; RU validates its own cleaning.
8. Premises and equipment: GMP-compliant, matched to SU or justified; qualification (DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ) and validation (process, cleaning, method).
9. QC: analytical method transfer; documentation controlled under QMS.
questions.question: Define technology transfer. Describe the WHO guidelines for technology transfer with terminology and the steps of transfer from R&D to production.

questions.answer:
1. Protocol: written plan approved by SU, RU and QA of both, describing how the transfer will be done and judged.
2. Contents: objective and scope; key personnel and responsibilities; description of product, process and methods; comparison of materials, equipment and facilities (gap analysis); risk assessment; training; number and size of trial and validation batches; sampling and tests; acceptance criteria; documents to be handed over; timeline; deviation handling.
3. Granularity = breaking the transfer into parts: API (route or supplier, specification, particle size, polymorph, solubility, stability, hazards, impurity profile); excipients (grade, supplier, functional properties such as HPMC viscosity grade or lactose particle size); finished product (formula, process flow, critical parameters, specifications, stability); packaging materials (specifications, drawings, suppliers, protection data).
4. Analytical method transfer: documented process showing the receiving laboratory can use a validated method.
5. Approaches: comparative testing (both labs test same lots); co-validation (RU takes part in validation); full or partial revalidation; transfer waiver (justified, e.g. a pharmacopoeial method already used).
6. Protocol for method transfer: method, samples, replicates, acceptance criteria, equivalence of reference standards, reagents, columns and instruments, investigation of failures.
7. Conclude: TT report records results and confirms success.
questions.question: What is a technology transfer protocol? Explain the granularity of the TT process and analytical method transfer.

questions.answer:
1. Commercialisation: taking a technology from the laboratory to the market and earning from it.
2. Practical aspects: market survey; cost and pricing; scale-up and TT; regulatory approval in each market; IP protection and licensing; funding, partners, distribution.
3. Problems: scale-up failure (e.g. weight variation at high press speed); equipment differences between sites; raw-material variation from a new supplier; incomplete transfer of tacit know-how; analytical mismatch; regulatory delays; cost overrun; IP disputes.
4. Case examples: capping solved by precompression and limited press speed; low assay at RU traced to shorter sonication; slower dissolution traced to finer lactose, fixed by tightening particle size specification.
5. APCTD/APCTT: Asian and Pacific Centre for Transfer of Technology, a regional institution of UN-ESCAP in New Delhi; capacity building and technology information for the region.
6. NRDC: National Research Development Corporation (1953, under DSIR); licenses technologies from national laboratories and universities to industry.
7. TIFAC: Technology Information, Forecasting and Assessment Council (1988, under DST); technology forecasting and technology-led projects.
8. BCIL: Biotech Consortium India Limited, promoted by DBT; biotechnology transfer, licensing, consultancy.
9. TBSE/SIDBI: Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises with SIDBI; helps small enterprises find technology, partners and finance.
questions.question: Discuss commercialisation of a technology with practical aspects and problems. Write a note on TT agencies in India.

questions.answer:
1. Confidentiality (non-disclosure) agreement: signed before sharing secrets; defines confidential information, permitted users and purpose, duration, return or destruction of information.
2. MoU: records intention to cooperate and broad terms (scope, responsibilities, timelines); usually less binding than a contract.
3. Licensing agreement: licensor allows licensee to use technology; terms: field and territory, exclusive or non-exclusive, duration and termination, payments (lump sum, milestones, royalties), ownership of improvements, quality obligations and audits, confidentiality.
4. TT and quality agreements: what is transferred, who files with regulators, GMP responsibilities.
5. Legal issues: patents, know-how, product liability, dispute resolution.

3. Blood sampling at planned times; validated bioanalytical method.

5. Acceptance: 90% CI of test/reference geometric mean ratio for AUC and Cmax within 80.00–125.00%.

# Unit 1: Pilot plant scale-up techniques

A formula that works in a 500 g laboratory batch does not automatically work in a 500 kg production batch. Mixing takes longer, heat moves more slowly through a large mass, granules dry unevenly and machines run much faster. The **pilot plant** is the bridge between the research laboratory and the factory floor, where a process is tried at an intermediate size so that these problems are found and solved before full production begins.

## 1.1 Definitions

- **Pilot plant:** a part of the pharmaceutical industry where a laboratory-scale formula is turned into a viable product by developing a reliable, practical and economical manufacturing procedure, using equipment similar in design to production equipment.
- **Scale-up:** the process of increasing the batch size (laboratory → pilot → production) while keeping the product quality the same.
- **Scale-down:** decreasing the batch size, for example to make a smaller batch for a small market, or to study a production problem at a convenient size.
- **Pilot-scale batch:** for solid oral dosage forms, a batch is commonly described as pilot scale when it is at least one-tenth (10%) of the full production batch or 100,000 units, whichever is larger. (This is the US FDA description used in SUPAC; check the guideline that applies to your product.)

```text
Laboratory (bench) scale  →  Pilot plant scale  →  Production (commercial) scale
   grams to a few kg           tens of kg             hundreds of kg to tonnes
   prove the formula          prove the process      routine manufacture
```

## 1.2 Objectives and significance of a pilot plant

**Objectives**

1. Try the laboratory formula and process on equipment that resembles production machines.
2. Find out which process variables (mixing time, granulating fluid, drying temperature, compression speed) are critical and fix their limits.
3. Produce batches for clinical trials, stability studies and regulatory submissions (exhibit or bio-batches).
4. Write the master manufacturing formula, process instructions and in-process controls for production.
5. Check that raw materials from approved suppliers behave the same from lot to lot.
6. Train production staff and transfer the process smoothly to the plant.
7. Estimate cost, yield and time of manufacture.

**Significance (why it matters)**

- Avoids costly failures of full-size batches.
- Gives data needed for validation and for the regulatory dossier.
- Shows whether a change in equipment or batch size will change the product.
- Allows the company to make enough product for clinical and stability work before the production line is ready.

## 1.3 General considerations

### a. Reporting responsibility

The pilot plant group works between Research and Development (R&D) and production. It reports to R&D for formulation matters and works closely with production, quality assurance, quality control, engineering and regulatory affairs. Clear lines of reporting are needed so that every change is documented and approved.

```text
             R&D (formulation)
                    │
          Pilot plant / scale-up group
         ┌────────┬─────────┬──────────┐
     Production  QA / QC   Engineering  Regulatory affairs
```

### b. Personnel requirements

The staff should have both theory and hands-on skill:

- Scientific knowledge of pharmaceutics, chemistry and engineering (often pharmacists, chemical engineers).
- Practical experience in the operation of production-type equipment.
- Ability to communicate with R&D, production and quality staff and to write clear reports.
- Understanding of GMP, documentation and validation.
- Knowledge of computers, data handling and process instruments.

### c. Space requirements

| Area | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Administration and information processing | Offices, records, data processing, report writing |
| Physical testing area | In-process and finished product tests (hardness, friability, viscosity, particle size) |
| Standard pilot-plant equipment floor | Production-type machines (mixers, granulators, dryers, tablet press, coaters, liquid tanks), arranged to allow cleaning and movement |
| Storage area | Separate areas for approved raw materials, quarantine, in-process material and finished pilot batches; controlled temperature and humidity where needed |

Space should be flexible, so equipment can be moved and new trials set up. Utilities (purified water, compressed air, steam, electrical supply, dust extraction, HVAC) must match production standards.

### d. Review of the formula

The laboratory formula is examined ingredient by ingredient: why each excipient is there, its grade and supplier, and whether its quantity can be produced reliably at a larger scale. Order of mixing, granulating fluid, drying and lubrication steps are reviewed.

### e. Raw materials

- Raw materials used in the laboratory may have come from small, specially selected lots. The pilot plant must test materials from the actual commercial suppliers.
- Physical properties (particle size, bulk density, moisture, flow, polymorphic form) can vary between suppliers and lots and may change the product.
- Specifications should be set for each material, and approved suppliers qualified.

### f. Relevant processing equipment

Equipment should be economical, simple, easy to clean and similar in principle to production machines. The size chosen should allow realistic shear, mixing and heat transfer.

### g. Production rates

The expected market demand decides the batch size and the number of batches per year. Equipment and process should be chosen to meet that rate without excessive overtime or idle capacity.

### h. Process evaluation (parameters studied)

1. Order of mixing of ingredients.
2. Mixing speed and mixing time.
3. Rate of addition of granulating agent, solvents or solutions of drug.
4. Heating and cooling rates.
5. Filter size (for liquids) and screen size (for solids).
6. Drying temperature and drying time.

### i. Master manufacturing procedures

These include the weighing sheet (each ingredient, quantity, lot number), processing directions in clear steps, equipment and settings, in-process checks with limits, sampling instructions, yields and signatures of the person who did each step and the person who checked it.

### j. Product stability and uniformity

Pilot batches are put on stability study and tested for content uniformity, because scale-up can change both.

### k. GMP considerations

Equipment qualification, process validation, regular calibration, cleaning and its validation, written procedures, change control, and orderly records are needed even in the pilot plant.

## 1.4 Pilot plant scale-up considerations for solids (tablets and capsules)

The main problems arise in handling and processing powders.

| Step | Scale-up points to study |
| --- | --- |
| Material handling | Small batches are handled by hand; large batches need bins, vacuum or gravity transfer. Dust control and segregation during transfer must be checked. |
| Dry blending | Blender type, load (fill volume), speed and time. Over-mixing can demix or coat particles with lubricant. Blend uniformity is tested with a sampling thief. |
| Granulation | Wet granulation in high-shear mixers is sensitive to impeller and chopper speed, fluid amount and rate, and end point (often judged by power consumption or torque). Dry granulation (slugging, roller compaction) needs control of roll pressure and gap. |
| Drying | Tray dryer vs fluid bed dryer; inlet air temperature, air flow, load, drying time; loss on drying end point. |
| Size reduction (milling) | Mill type, screen size, speed; granule size distribution affects flow and weight variation. |
| Blending and lubrication | Lubricant (e.g. magnesium stearate) mixing time is critical; too long reduces hardness and slows dissolution. |
| Compression | Machine speed (dwell time) on high-speed rotary presses, feeder type (forced feeders), punch and die tooling, precompression, hardness, weight control. Problems such as capping and sticking may appear only at high speed. |
| Coating | Pan size and speed, spray rate, atomising air, inlet temperature, number of guns, tablet load. |
| Capsule filling | Change from hand or semi-automatic filling to automatic dosator or tamping machines; powder flow and plug formation must suit the machine. |

```text
Weigh → dry mix → wet granulate → dry → mill → blend + lubricate → compress → coat → pack
   ↑         ↑            ↑          ↑       ↑           ↑               ↑
 order    time/speed   fluid, end  temp,   screen   lubricant time   speed, dwell
                       point       airflow  size                     time, hardness
```

## 1.5 Scale-up considerations for liquid orals

Liquid orals (solutions, syrups, suspensions, emulsions) look simple, but scale-up still needs care.

1. **Equipment:** jacketed stainless-steel tanks with suitable agitators, homogenisers or colloid mills for emulsions and suspensions, filtration units, transfer pumps and filling machines.
2. **Mixing:** the type of agitator, speed, and position of the impeller change with tank size. Solids must dissolve or be wetted completely; over-agitation can trap air.
3. **Order of addition and temperature:** for example, dissolving sugar with heat for syrups, adding preservative at the right temperature, and adding flavour after cooling so it is not lost.
4. **Heating and cooling time:** a large tank takes much longer to heat and cool, which can increase degradation or microbial growth.
5. **Filtration:** filter type and area, pressure, and clarity must be checked; filters must not adsorb preservatives.
6. **Suspensions:** particle size of the solid, wetting, viscosity of the vehicle, sedimentation volume and ease of redispersion. Homogenisation may be needed.
7. **Emulsions:** phase volume, emulsifier, temperature of each phase, rate of addition, and homogenisation pressure decide globule size.
8. **Physical stability checks:** appearance, colour, odour, taste, pH, viscosity, specific gravity, sedimentation and creaming.
9. **Microbial control:** clean, sanitised equipment and suitable water quality; preservative efficacy.
10. **Filling:** fill volume accuracy, foaming, and compatibility with containers and closures.

## 1.6 Scale-up considerations for semisolids

For ointments, creams, gels and pastes:

1. **Mixing equipment:** jacketed vessels with anchor (scraping) agitators plus high-shear homogenisers; vacuum mixing to avoid air entrapment.
2. **Heating and cooling rates:** the melting of the fatty phase, the temperature at which phases are combined, and the cooling rate affect consistency and crystal formation.
3. **Shear and mixing time:** too much shear can break the structure of some gels; too little leaves lumps or poor drug distribution.
4. **Incorporation of the drug:** dissolved or dispersed; particle size of a dispersed drug must be controlled (milling or levigation).
5. **Transfer and pumping:** viscous products need suitable pumps and pipes; air pockets must be prevented.
6. **Filling:** tubes or jars; filling temperature affects flow and final consistency.
7. **Tests:** appearance, homogeneity, viscosity and rheology, spreadability, pH, drug content, and stability under heat and cold.

## 1.7 Relevant documentation

Pilot plant work is useful only if it is written down well. Typical documents:

| Document | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Master formula record (master manufacturing formula) | Product name, strength, batch size, list of ingredients with quantities and grades, equipment, process steps, in-process controls, yield limits |
| Batch manufacturing record | The actual record of one batch: lot numbers, weights, times, settings, results and signatures |
| Scale-up / development report | What was tried, problems found, critical parameters and the reasons for the final process |
| Raw material specifications | Tests and limits for each excipient and the API |
| In-process and finished product specifications | Tests, methods and limits |
| Standard operating procedures | Operation, cleaning and calibration of each machine |
| Process validation protocol and report | Plan and results showing the process gives consistent quality |
| Stability protocol and data | Storage conditions, time points, results |
| Change control records | Any change after the process is fixed |

## 1.8 SUPAC guidelines

**SUPAC** stands for **Scale-Up and Post-Approval Changes**. These are guidance documents of the US FDA that tell a company what tests and what kind of filing are needed when it changes an already approved product. The aim is to keep quality and performance the same while allowing reasonable changes.

**The SUPAC family**

| Guideline | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| SUPAC-IR | Immediate-release solid oral dosage forms |
| SUPAC-MR | Modified-release solid oral dosage forms |
| SUPAC-SS | Non-sterile semisolid dosage forms (creams, ointments, gels, lotions) |

**Types of change covered**

1. Components and composition (excipient amounts).
2. Site of manufacture.
3. Batch size (scale-up or scale-down).
4. Manufacturing equipment.
5. Manufacturing process.

**Levels of change**

| Level | Meaning | Usual reporting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level 1 | Unlikely to have any detectable effect on quality and performance | Annual report |
| Level 2 | Could have a significant effect | A supplement to the application (the type depends on the change) |
| Level 3 | Likely to have a significant effect | Prior approval supplement, with more testing (sometimes bioequivalence) |

**Examples**

- Batch size: an increase up to about ten times the pilot or bio-batch, using equipment of the same design and operating principle, is a Level 1 change; beyond ten times is Level 2.
- Excipients: a small change in the amount of an excipient, within limits set for each excipient class (filler, disintegrant, binder, lubricant, glidant, film coat), is Level 1; a larger but limited change is Level 2; anything bigger, or a change in excipient type, is Level 3.
- Equipment: change to equipment of the same design and operating principle is Level 1; change to a different design and principle is Level 2.
- Site (SUPAC-IR): a move within the same facility is Level 1; within the same contiguous campus is Level 2; to a different campus is Level 3.

**Tests required** depend on level and BCS class of the drug: stability data (long-term and accelerated), dissolution profiles in one or several media compared with the earlier product (similarity factor f2 between 50 and 100 shows similar profiles), and in vivo bioequivalence for some Level 3 changes.

**Equipment addendum:** a companion FDA document classifies manufacturing equipment (blenders, granulators, dryers, mills, presses, coaters) into classes and subclasses by operating principle and design, so a company can decide whether a new machine counts as "same" or "different".

Note: SUPAC is a US guideline. Indian manufacturers follow it for products exported to the USA. In India, post-approval changes are handled under the Drugs and Cosmetics rules and CDSCO notices; check the current CDSCO guidance before filing any change.

## 1.9 Introduction to platform technology

A **platform technology** is a proven, reusable system or process that can be applied to many different drugs or products with only small changes, rather than inventing a new process for each product.

**Examples**

| Platform | How it is reused |
| --- | --- |
| Osmotic pump tablets (OROS type) | Same push–pull design used for different drugs needing controlled release |
| Matrix tablets of hydrophilic polymers (e.g. HPMC) | Same polymer system and process for many once-daily tablets |
| Liposomes, nanoparticles, solid lipid particles | Same carrier and process for different drugs |
| Hot-melt extrusion / solid dispersions | Same process to improve solubility of many poorly soluble drugs |
| Orally disintegrating tablet technologies | Same base and process for many drugs |
| Prefilled syringes, auto-injectors, inhalers | Same device for several drugs |
| Monoclonal antibody manufacturing platform | Same cell line type, purification steps and analytical methods for many antibodies |
| mRNA and viral-vector vaccine platforms | Same production and delivery system, new antigen code |

**Advantages**

1. Shorter development time and lower cost.
2. Existing knowledge, equipment and validated processes are reused.
3. Lower technical risk, since the platform has worked before.
4. Easier regulatory review where earlier data support the new product.
5. Faster scale-up and technology transfer.

**Limitations:** not every drug suits a platform; patents may restrict use; each new product still needs its own data on quality, safety and efficacy.

## Remember

- Pilot plant = intermediate stage between laboratory and production where a reliable, economical process is developed on production-like equipment.
- Pilot-scale batch for solid orals: at least 10% of production batch or 100,000 units, whichever is larger (FDA SUPAC description).
- General considerations: reporting responsibility, personnel, space (administration, physical testing, equipment floor, storage), formula review, raw materials, equipment, production rates, process evaluation, master manufacturing procedures, stability, GMP.
- Solids: blending, granulation end point, drying, milling, lubrication time, compression speed and dwell time.
- Liquids: agitation, order of addition, heating/cooling rates, filtration, homogenisation, filling.
- Semisolids: heating/cooling, shear, vacuum mixing, transfer of viscous mass.
- SUPAC (FDA): IR, MR, SS; changes in components, site, batch size, equipment, process; Levels 1, 2, 3; f2 50–100 = similar dissolution.
- Platform technology = a reusable delivery or manufacturing system applied to many products.

# Unit 2: Technology development and transfer

A new product is usually developed in one place (an R&D laboratory or pilot plant) and made in another (a production plant, often in another city or country, sometimes by a different company). Moving the knowledge, documents and skills needed to make the product reliably at the new place is called **technology transfer (TT)**. If it is done badly, the receiving plant makes batches that fail, and the product reaches patients late or not at all.

## 2.1 Definition and purpose

**Technology transfer** is a logical procedure that controls the transfer of any process, together with its documentation and professional expertise, between development and manufacture or between manufacturing sites.

Purpose:

1. To make the product at the new site with the same quality, safety and efficacy as at the original site.
2. To move the product from R&D to commercial production (vertical transfer) or from one plant to another (horizontal transfer).
3. To license a product or process to another company (in-licensing / out-licensing), or to a contract manufacturer.
4. To share know-how between public research bodies and industry.

**Types**

| Type | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Vertical (development to production) | R&D formula → company's own plant |
| Horizontal (site to site) | One plant → another plant of the same company |
| Inter-company | Innovator → licensee or contract manufacturer |
| Public to private | Government laboratory → industry, through agencies such as NRDC |
| International | Foreign company → Indian manufacturer, or the reverse |

## 2.2 WHO guidelines for technology transfer

The World Health Organization published **WHO guidelines on transfer of technology in pharmaceutical manufacturing** in its Technical Report Series (TRS No. 961, Annex 7, 2011). They cover transfer of the API, excipients, finished products and packaging, analytical methods, premises and equipment, qualification and validation, and documentation. Check the WHO website for any later revision before quoting it in a dossier.

### Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Sending unit (SU) | The site or party that holds the technology and sends it |
| Receiving unit (RU) | The site or party that receives the technology and will make the product |
| Technology transfer team | Members of SU and RU from R&D, production, QA, QC, engineering and regulatory affairs, with a named leader |
| Technology transfer protocol | The agreed written plan for the transfer |
| Technology transfer report | The written record of what was done, results and conclusions |
| Critical quality attribute (CQA) | A property of the product that must stay within limits to ensure quality |
| Critical process parameter (CPP) | A process setting that affects a CQA and must be controlled |
| Design space | The range of material and process variables shown to give acceptable quality |
| Acceptance criteria | Numerical limits or conditions that decide whether the transfer succeeded |
| Gap analysis | Comparison of SU and RU capabilities to find differences that need action |
| Quality risk management (QRM) | Systematic assessment, control, communication and review of risks to quality |
| Commissioning | Setting up and testing new equipment or a facility before qualification |

### Principles of a successful transfer

1. The transfer must be planned, documented and approved.
2. The RU must have the capacity, skills and facilities to make the product.
3. Both units agree on acceptance criteria before work begins.
4. All differences between SU and RU (equipment, materials, environment, procedures) are identified and their risk assessed.
5. The transfer is complete only when the RU shows, with data, that it can repeat the process and meet all specifications.

## 2.3 Technology transfer protocol

The protocol is written jointly and approved by both SU and RU (and QA of each). It usually lists:

1. Objective and scope of the transfer.
2. Key personnel and their responsibilities.
3. Description of the product, process and analytical methods to be transferred.
4. Comparison of materials, equipment, facilities and procedures at SU and RU (gap analysis).
5. Risk assessment and planned controls.
6. Training needed at the RU.
7. Experimental design: number and size of batches (trial and validation), sampling plan, tests.
8. Acceptance criteria for each step.
9. Documents to be handed over.
10. Timeline and how deviations will be handled.

```text
Plan and form team → gap analysis + risk assessment → protocol approved
   → document and knowledge transfer → training at RU
   → analytical method transfer → trial batches → validation batches
   → stability data → TT report → regulatory filing → routine production
```

## 2.4 Quality risk management in technology transfer

Risk management (described in ICH Q9) means finding what could go wrong, how likely and how serious it is, and controlling it.

- **Risk assessment:** risk identification, risk analysis, risk evaluation.
- **Risk control:** reduce the risk or accept it with justification.
- **Risk communication and review:** share findings and review them as data arrive.

Tools: FMEA (failure mode and effects analysis), fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, HACCP, fault tree analysis, risk ranking. In TT, typical risks are a different grade of excipient, a different granulator design, different water quality, or less experienced operators. Each is scored and given a control (extra testing, more trial batches, training, equipment change).

## 2.5 Transfer from R&D to production

### a. Process transfer

The SU hands over the development report, master formula, process description with critical parameters and their ranges, in-process controls, batch records from development and pilot batches, stability data, and known problems with their solutions. The RU prepares its own master batch record for its equipment, makes trial batches, then validation batches.

### b. Packaging transfer

The SU gives specifications of primary and secondary packaging materials (type of container, closure, blister film, foil), packaging design, compatibility and stability data in that pack, and any special needs (desiccant, light protection, child-resistant closure). The RU checks its packaging line can handle the pack and qualifies its suppliers.

### c. Cleaning

Information on the product's solubility, toxicity, potency (for setting residue limits), cleaning agents, cleaning procedures and validated analytical methods for residues is transferred. The RU writes and validates its own cleaning procedure, considering other products made on the same equipment.

## 2.6 Granularity of the TT process

"Granularity" means breaking the transfer into its separate pieces, each with its own information:

| Item | Information transferred |
| --- | --- |
| API (drug substance) | Route of synthesis or supplier, specifications, physical properties (particle size, polymorphic form, solubility), stability, storage, handling hazards (potent or toxic), impurity profile |
| Excipients | Grade, specification, supplier, functional properties that affect the product (e.g. viscosity grade of HPMC, particle size of lactose), any animal-origin concerns |
| Finished product | Formula, process flow, critical parameters, in-process and release specifications, stability, known variability |
| Packaging materials | Specifications, drawings, suppliers, compatibility and protection data |

## 2.7 Documentation

Typical documents in a transfer:

- Technology transfer protocol and report.
- Development report (formulation and process history, justification of formula).
- Master formula and batch manufacturing records.
- Specifications and test methods (API, excipients, packaging, in-process, finished product).
- Validation and qualification protocols and reports.
- Stability protocols and data.
- Standard operating procedures.
- Risk assessment reports and gap analysis.
- Training records.

All documents must be controlled (version, approval, distribution) under the quality system.

## 2.8 Premises and equipment

- The RU's premises should meet GMP and the needs of the product (for example humidity control for hygroscopic drugs, containment for potent drugs, clean rooms for sterile products).
- Equipment should be compared with the SU's: same operating principle and capacity, or differences justified with data. Different equipment may need changes in process settings.
- A list of SU equipment with make, model and settings helps the RU match them.

## 2.9 Qualification and validation

- **Qualification** shows that equipment and utilities are suitable: design qualification (DQ), installation qualification (IQ), operational qualification (OQ), performance qualification (PQ).
- **Process validation** shows that the process consistently gives a product meeting its specifications. Traditionally three consecutive successful batches at commercial scale are made; current approaches use the product life cycle (process design, process qualification, continued process verification).
- **Cleaning validation** and **analytical method validation** are also needed.
- Validation is done only after the equipment is qualified and the analytical methods are transferred.

## 2.10 Quality control and analytical method transfer

The RU's QC laboratory must be able to run every test method and obtain the same results as the SU.

**Analytical method transfer** is the documented process that shows a receiving laboratory can use a validated method as intended.

Approaches:

| Approach | What is done |
| --- | --- |
| Comparative testing | Both laboratories test the same lots; results compared against preset criteria |
| Co-validation | The RU takes part in the validation of the method itself |
| Revalidation (full or partial) | The RU repeats the validation parameters relevant to it |
| Transfer waiver | Justified exemption, e.g. a simple pharmacopoeial method already used by the RU |

The protocol states the method, samples, number of replicates, acceptance criteria (for example difference in mean assay results within an agreed limit) and how failures are investigated. Reference standards, reagents, columns and instruments must be equivalent.

## 2.11 Approved regulatory bodies and agencies

Transfers that change the manufacturing site of an approved product must be reported to the regulator of each market. Examples of regulatory bodies whose rules affect TT:

| Country / region | Body |
| --- | --- |
| India | Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) and State Licensing Authorities |
| USA | Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) |
| European Union | European Medicines Agency (EMA) with national agencies |
| United Kingdom | Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) |
| Japan | Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) |
| Australia | Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) |
| Canada | Health Canada |
| Global guidance | WHO (prequalification, GMP), ICH (harmonised guidelines) |

## 2.12 Commercialisation: practical aspects and problems

**Commercialisation** is taking a technology from the laboratory to the market and earning from it.

Practical aspects:

1. Market survey and demand.
2. Cost of production and pricing.
3. Scale-up and technology transfer.
4. Regulatory approval in each market.
5. Intellectual property (patents, licences).
6. Funding, partners and distribution network.

Common problems:

| Problem | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Scale-up failure | A granule that flows well at pilot scale gives weight variation on a high-speed press |
| Equipment differences | RU has a fluid bed granulator where the SU used a high-shear mixer |
| Raw-material variation | A new supplier's excipient has a different particle size |
| Incomplete knowledge transfer | Tacit "tricks" of the SU staff not written down |
| Analytical differences | RU gets lower assay because of a different column or standard handling |
| Regulatory delays | Site-change approval takes longer than planned |
| Cost overrun | Extra trial batches and validation |
| Legal and IP issues | Disputes over ownership of improvements |

**Short case studies (illustrative)**

- *Case 1 — tablet capping after transfer:* a tablet made well at the SU capped at the RU. The gap analysis had missed that the RU press ran much faster. Solution: precompression added and press speed limited in the master record.
- *Case 2 — assay mismatch:* RU's assay results were consistently lower. Investigation found incomplete extraction because the RU used a shorter sonication time; the method was written more precisely and the transfer repeated.
- *Case 3 — dissolution failure:* a new excipient supplier's lactose had a finer particle size; tablets were harder and dissolved more slowly. The excipient specification was tightened to include particle size.

## 2.13 Technology transfer agencies in India

| Agency | Full name | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| APCTD / APCTT | Asian and Pacific Centre for Transfer of Technology (a regional institution of UN-ESCAP, based in New Delhi; the syllabus spells it APCTD) | Helps member countries of the Asia-Pacific region to build capacity for technology transfer, shares information on technologies and supports small enterprises |
| NRDC | National Research Development Corporation (set up by the Government of India in 1953; under the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research) | Licenses technologies developed in national research laboratories and universities to industry; helps with patents and commercialisation |
| TIFAC | Technology Information, Forecasting and Assessment Council (an autonomous body under the Department of Science and Technology, set up in 1988) | Technology forecasting and assessment (e.g. Technology Vision documents), supports technology-led projects with industry |
| BCIL | Biotech Consortium India Limited (promoted by the Department of Biotechnology) | Transfers and commercialises biotechnology; helps with patents, licensing, project consultancy and biosafety |
| TBSE / SIDBI | Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises, a joint initiative involving the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) | Helps small and medium enterprises find technologies, partners and finance |

## 2.14 TT-related documentation: agreements and legal issues

### a. Confidentiality agreement (non-disclosure agreement, NDA in the legal sense)

Signed before any secret information is shared. It defines what is confidential, who may see it, for what purpose, for how long, and what happens to the information if talks fail. (Do not confuse it with the New Drug Application, also abbreviated NDA.)

### b. Memorandum of understanding (MoU)

A document recording the intention of the parties to work together and the broad terms (scope, responsibilities, timelines). It is usually not as binding as a formal contract but guides the later agreement.

### c. Licensing agreement

The owner of a technology (licensor) gives another party (licensee) the right to use it, often in exchange for an upfront payment and royalties. Terms include:

- Field and territory (which products, which countries).
- Exclusive or non-exclusive rights.
- Duration and termination.
- Payments: lump sum, milestones, royalty on sales.
- Ownership of improvements.
- Quality obligations and audits.
- Confidentiality.

### d. Technology transfer agreement / supply and quality agreements

Defines what will be transferred, timelines, responsibilities for regulatory filings, and a quality (technical) agreement describing who is responsible for which GMP activity.

### e. Legal issues

- Patents and other intellectual property rights (who owns what, freedom to operate).
- Trade secrets and know-how protection.
- Breach of confidentiality.
- Product liability.
- Competition law and export controls.
- Dispute resolution (arbitration, governing law and jurisdiction).

## Remember

- Technology transfer = documented transfer of process, documents and know-how between development and manufacture or between sites; success = RU repeatedly meets all specifications.
- WHO TT guideline: TRS 961, Annex 7 (2011). Key terms: sending unit, receiving unit, protocol, report, gap analysis, CQA, CPP, design space.
- Protocol: objective, team, gap analysis, risk assessment, training, batches, acceptance criteria, timeline.
- QRM (ICH Q9): identify → analyse → evaluate → control → communicate → review; FMEA, fishbone.
- R&D → production covers process, packaging and cleaning; granularity covers API, excipients, finished product, packaging.
- Qualification DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ; then process, cleaning and method validation.
- Method transfer: comparative testing, co-validation, revalidation, waiver.
- Indian TT agencies: APCTD/APCTT, NRDC, TIFAC, BCIL, TBSE/SIDBI.
- Documents: confidentiality agreement, MoU, licensing agreement, TT and quality agreements; legal issues = IP, know-how, liability, disputes.

# Unit 3: Regulatory affairs and regulatory requirements for drug approval

No medicine can be sold until a government regulator is satisfied that it is safe, effective and of good quality. **Regulatory affairs (RA)** is the profession that sits between the company and the regulator: it plans what data are needed, collects them from every department, presents them in the required format and keeps the product compliant for as long as it is on the market.

This unit has two halves: regulatory affairs as a function (Part A) and the data and documents needed to get a new drug approved, using the US FDA system named in the syllabus as the model (Part B).

## Part A: Regulatory affairs

## 3.1 Introduction and definition

**Regulatory affairs** is the function in a pharmaceutical company that ensures its products, processes and activities comply with the laws, regulations and guidelines of every country where it operates, from early development through approval to post-marketing.

Scope of RA:

1. Drug development strategy from a regulatory point of view.
2. Preparation and submission of applications (clinical trial, marketing, variations, renewals).
3. Communication with regulators (meetings, queries, inspections).
4. Labelling and promotional material review.
5. Post-approval changes and life-cycle management.
6. Pharmacovigilance and safety reporting support.
7. Keeping track of new laws and guidelines (regulatory intelligence).

## 3.2 Historical overview of regulatory affairs

Most drug laws were written after a disaster showed that the earlier law was not enough.

| Year | Event | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1906 | USA: unsafe and mislabelled foods and drugs | Pure Food and Drugs Act — banned adulterated and misbranded products |
| 1937–38 | USA: "Elixir Sulfanilamide" made with diethylene glycol killed over a hundred people | Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act 1938 — proof of **safety** required before marketing |
| Late 1950s–1962 | Thalidomide, used in pregnancy, caused severe limb defects in thousands of babies, mainly in Europe | USA: Kefauver–Harris Amendments 1962 — proof of **efficacy** as well as safety; informed consent; GMP |
| 1964 | World Medical Association | Declaration of Helsinki — ethics of research on humans |
| 1984 | USA | Hatch–Waxman Act — Abbreviated NDA (ANDA) route for generics, patent term restoration |
| 1990 | Regulators and industry of USA, EU and Japan | International Council (then Conference) for Harmonisation, ICH — common guidelines (Q, S, E, M series) |
| 1995 | Europe | European Medicines Agency (EMA, first called EMEA) begins work |

**India**

| Year | Law |
| --- | --- |
| 1940 | Drugs and Cosmetics Act (originally the Drugs Act) |
| 1945 | Drugs and Cosmetics Rules |
| 1948 | Pharmacy Act |
| 1954 | Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act |
| 1985 | Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act |
| 2019 | New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules (replaced the earlier Schedule Y provisions for new drugs and trials) |

## 3.3 Regulatory authorities

| Country / region | Authority |
| --- | --- |
| India | CDSCO, headed by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) |
| USA | Food and Drug Administration (FDA) |
| European Union | European Medicines Agency (EMA) and national competent authorities |
| United Kingdom | MHRA |
| Japan | Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare with PMDA |
| Australia | Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) |
| Canada | Health Canada |
| China | National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) |
| Global | WHO (guidelines, prequalification), ICH (harmonised technical guidelines) |

## 3.4 Role of the regulatory affairs department

```text
         R&D ──┐
     Clinical ─┤
   Production ─┤──→  REGULATORY AFFAIRS  ──→  Regulators (CDSCO, FDA, EMA …)
     QA / QC ──┤          ↑      │
   Marketing ──┘   queries│      │approvals, conditions
                          └──────┘
```

Roles:

1. **Strategy:** advise management which markets, which route (new drug, generic, 505(b)(2)), what studies are needed and how long approval may take.
2. **Dossier preparation:** collect, check and compile data in CTD/eCTD format.
3. **Submission and follow-up:** file applications, answer queries, attend meetings.
4. **Labelling:** prepare and check package inserts, labels and patient information.
5. **Life-cycle management:** variations, renewals, new indications, new strengths.
6. **Compliance:** check that manufacturing and promotion follow approved conditions; support inspections.
7. **Regulatory intelligence:** watch new rules and inform departments.
8. **Training** of staff on regulatory requirements.

## 3.5 Responsibilities of a regulatory affairs professional

- Know current regulations and guidelines of the target markets.
- Plan and track submissions and timelines.
- Ensure data are complete, accurate and consistent across modules.
- Write clear summaries and responses to queries.
- Maintain records of all submissions and approvals.
- Review change controls for regulatory impact.
- Review labels and promotional material.
- Communicate honestly with regulators and keep confidential information safe.
- Support pharmacovigilance reporting.
- Skills needed: scientific knowledge, attention to detail, writing, negotiation, project management.

## Part B: Regulatory requirements for drug approval

## 3.6 Overview of drug development

```text
Discovery → Preclinical (non-clinical) → IND → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III
          → NDA / marketing application → Review and approval → Phase IV (post-marketing)
```

It commonly takes 10–15 years from discovery to approval, and only a small fraction of molecules entering trials are finally approved.

## 3.7 Drug development teams

Drug development is done by cross-functional teams:

| Team member | Contribution |
| --- | --- |
| Discovery / medicinal chemists | Design and synthesis of the molecule |
| Pharmacologists | Efficacy and mechanism studies |
| Toxicologists | Safety studies in animals |
| DMPK scientists | Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion |
| Formulation scientists | Dosage form development |
| Analytical scientists | Methods, specifications, stability |
| Process chemists and engineers | Scale-up of API and product |
| Clinical team (physicians, clinical research associates) | Design and conduct of trials |
| Biostatisticians and data managers | Study design, analysis, data quality |
| Regulatory affairs | Strategy and submissions |
| QA | Compliance with GLP, GCP, GMP |
| Project manager | Timelines, budget, coordination |

## 3.8 Non-clinical drug development

Non-clinical (preclinical) studies are done in vitro and in animals before and alongside human trials, under **Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)**.

### a. Pharmacology

- **Primary pharmacodynamics:** effect on the intended target and in disease models.
- **Secondary pharmacodynamics:** effects on other targets.
- **Safety pharmacology:** effects on vital systems — cardiovascular (including QT prolongation, hERG assay), central nervous system and respiratory system (the "core battery").

### b. Drug metabolism and pharmacokinetics

- Absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME) in animal species.
- Metabolic pathways and metabolites, enzymes involved (CYP450), enzyme induction or inhibition.
- Plasma protein binding, tissue distribution.
- **Toxicokinetics:** drug exposure in toxicity studies, to relate toxicity to exposure.

### c. Toxicology

| Study | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Single-dose (acute) toxicity | Effects after one dose; helps choose doses for longer studies |
| Repeated-dose toxicity (subacute, subchronic, chronic) | Target organs and no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL); duration linked to proposed trial duration |
| Genotoxicity | Mutations and chromosome damage (Ames test, chromosomal aberration, micronucleus) |
| Carcinogenicity | For drugs taken long term |
| Reproductive and developmental toxicity | Fertility, embryo–fetal development, pre- and post-natal development |
| Local tolerance | Irritation at the site of application or injection |
| Immunotoxicity, special studies | Where needed |

Results are used to choose a safe starting dose for the first human study and to decide what to monitor.

## 3.9 Investigational New Drug (IND) application

An **IND** is the application to the US FDA for permission to give an unapproved drug to humans and to ship it across state lines for clinical trials. (Rules are in the US Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR Part 312.)

**Types of IND**

1. **Investigator IND:** filed by a physician who starts and conducts a study himself.
2. **Emergency use IND:** for urgent use in a situation that does not allow time for a normal application.
3. **Treatment IND:** for promising drugs for serious or life-threatening conditions while final trials are going on.
4. **Commercial IND:** filed by a company planning to market the drug.

**General considerations / contents**

1. Cover form (Form FDA 1571) and table of contents.
2. Introductory statement and general investigational plan.
3. Investigator's Brochure.
4. Clinical protocols for the planned studies.
5. Chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC) information.
6. Pharmacology and toxicology data.
7. Previous human experience, if any.
8. Statement of the investigator (Form FDA 1572) and other information.

If the FDA does not place a clinical hold within 30 days of receiving the IND, the trial may begin. During the IND the sponsor files protocol amendments, information amendments, safety reports and annual reports.

## 3.10 Investigator's Brochure (IB)

The **Investigator's Brochure** is a compilation of the clinical and non-clinical data on the investigational product that are relevant to its study in humans. It helps investigators understand the drug, the reasons for the protocol, and how to manage the subjects safely. (Its contents are described in ICH E6, Good Clinical Practice.)

Contents:

1. Title page and confidentiality statement.
2. Summary.
3. Introduction.
4. Physical, chemical and pharmaceutical properties and formulation.
5. Non-clinical studies (pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, toxicology).
6. Effects in humans (pharmacokinetics, safety, efficacy, marketing experience if any).
7. Summary of data and guidance for the investigator (risks, adverse reactions expected, precautions, monitoring).

The IB is reviewed and updated at least once a year and when important new information appears.

## 3.11 New Drug Application (NDA)

An **NDA** is the application to the US FDA to approve a new drug for marketing. It must show that the drug is safe and effective for the proposed use, that its benefits outweigh its risks, that the labelling is appropriate, and that manufacturing methods and controls maintain its identity, strength, quality and purity. (Rules in 21 CFR Part 314; the application form is Form FDA 356h.)

**Application routes in the USA**

| Route | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| 505(b)(1) "full" NDA | New molecule with full safety and efficacy data from the applicant's own studies |
| 505(b)(2) NDA | New product relying partly on published data or on FDA's earlier findings (new salt, dosage form, combination) |
| 505(j) ANDA | Generic copy shown to be bioequivalent to the reference listed drug; no new clinical efficacy trials |
| BLA | Biological products (under the Public Health Service Act) |

**NDA content (in CTD format)**

1. Administrative information, forms and proposed labelling.
2. Summaries (quality, non-clinical, clinical).
3. Chemistry, manufacturing and controls.
4. Non-clinical pharmacology and toxicology reports.
5. Human pharmacokinetics and bioavailability.
6. Clinical study reports (efficacy and safety), statistics.
7. Patent information, financial disclosure of investigators.
8. Samples, methods validation package, case report forms and tabulations.

**Review:** the FDA checks completeness (filing), reviews each discipline, may inspect manufacturing sites and clinical sites, may consult an advisory committee, and then issues an approval letter or a complete response letter listing deficiencies. Standard and priority reviews have different target times under user-fee goals; check the current FDA figures.

## 3.12 Clinical research and BE studies

### a. Phases of clinical trials

| Phase | Subjects | Main aim |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase 0 (exploratory, micro-dosing) | Very few volunteers | Early human PK at sub-therapeutic doses |
| Phase I | Usually healthy volunteers (patients for toxic drugs such as anticancer agents); small numbers | Safety, tolerability, PK, dose range |
| Phase II | Patients with the disease; a few hundred | Efficacy, dose finding, short-term safety |
| Phase III | Larger groups of patients, often multicentre | Confirm efficacy and safety against placebo or standard drug |
| Phase IV | Patients after approval | Post-marketing surveillance, rare adverse reactions, new uses |

### b. Bioavailability and bioequivalence (BE) studies

- **Bioavailability:** the rate and extent to which the active drug is absorbed and becomes available at the site of action.
- **Bioequivalence:** two pharmaceutically equivalent products show no significant difference in rate and extent of absorption when given at the same molar dose under similar conditions.

Typical BE study:

1. Healthy adult volunteers (after informed consent), usually a randomised, two-period, two-sequence crossover design.
2. Single dose of test and reference products, separated by a washout period long enough for the drug to be eliminated (commonly at least five half-lives).
3. Blood samples at planned times; drug measured by a validated bioanalytical method.
4. Parameters: Cmax (peak concentration), Tmax (time to peak), AUC0–t and AUC0–∞ (extent).
5. Acceptance: the 90% confidence interval of the test/reference ratio of the geometric means of AUC and Cmax should lie within 80.00–125.00% (wider limits are allowed in special cases by some regulators).

BE studies support generic approval (ANDA) and some post-approval changes.

### c. Good Clinical Practice (GCP)

GCP (ICH E6) is the international ethical and scientific standard for designing, conducting, recording and reporting trials. Key principles: rights, safety and well-being of subjects come first; informed consent; independent ethics committee approval; qualified investigators; accurate records; investigational product made under GMP; quality systems.

## 3.13 Clinical research protocols

A **protocol** is the document that describes the objectives, design, method, statistics and organisation of a trial.

Contents:

1. Title, protocol number, version and date; sponsor and investigators.
2. Background and rationale.
3. Objectives (primary, secondary) and endpoints.
4. Study design: randomisation, blinding (single, double), control (placebo or active), parallel or crossover.
5. Selection of subjects: inclusion and exclusion criteria, withdrawal criteria.
6. Treatment: dose, route, duration, concomitant medicines.
7. Assessment of efficacy and of safety; schedule of visits and tests.
8. Adverse event recording and reporting.
9. Statistics: sample size calculation, analysis plan, handling of missing data.
10. Data handling, record keeping, quality control and audit.
11. Ethics: ethics committee approval, informed consent.
12. Financing, insurance, compensation, publication policy.

## 3.14 Biostatistics in pharmaceutical product development

Statistics are needed at every stage:

| Stage | Statistical use |
| --- | --- |
| Formulation and process development | Design of experiments (factorial designs, response surfaces), process capability |
| Quality control | Sampling plans, control charts, specification limits |
| Stability | Regression analysis to estimate shelf life |
| BE studies | ANOVA, 90% confidence intervals, log transformation |
| Clinical trials | Sample size and power, randomisation, hypothesis testing |

Key terms:

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** no difference between treatments. **Alternative (H1):** there is a difference.
- **Type I error (α):** rejecting a true H0 (false positive); usually set at 0.05.
- **Type II error (β):** accepting a false H0 (false negative). **Power = 1 − β**, usually 80–90%.
- **p-value:** probability of obtaining the observed result (or more extreme) if H0 were true; p < 0.05 is taken as significant.
- **Confidence interval:** a range likely to contain the true value (e.g. 95% CI).
- **Tests:** t-test (two means), ANOVA (more than two means), chi-square (proportions), non-parametric tests for non-normal data.
- **Intention-to-treat analysis:** all randomised subjects analysed in the groups assigned.

## 3.15 Data presentation for FDA submissions

- Data are submitted electronically in the **eCTD** (electronic Common Technical Document) structure.
- Clinical study reports follow **ICH E3** (structure and content of clinical study reports).
- Data sets follow **CDISC** standards (SDTM for collected data, ADaM for analysis data) so reviewers can re-analyse them.
- Results are shown as **tables, listings and figures (TLFs):** demographic tables, efficacy tables with confidence intervals, adverse event tables, laboratory shift tables, Kaplan–Meier plots, forest plots.
- Integrated summaries of safety and efficacy pool all studies.
- Presentation must be clear, consistent across sections, traceable to the raw data, and honest about missing data and protocol deviations.

## 3.16 Management of clinical studies

Roles:

| Party | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor | Starts, funds and manages the trial; selects investigators; monitors; reports safety; may delegate to a CRO |
| Contract research organisation (CRO) | Carries out sponsor's tasks under contract |
| Investigator | Conducts the trial at the site; protects subjects; obtains consent; keeps records |
| Ethics committee | Reviews and approves protocol and consent; monitors subject safety |
| Regulator | Grants permission; inspects |
| Monitor (clinical research associate) | Visits sites, checks data against source documents and GCP compliance |

Steps in managing a trial:

```text
Feasibility and site selection → approvals (regulator + ethics committee)
→ investigator meeting and training → site initiation → subject recruitment and consent
→ treatment and data collection (CRF/eCRF) → monitoring visits → adverse event reporting
→ database lock → statistical analysis → clinical study report → archiving
```

Important controls: drug accountability, randomisation codes, serious adverse event reporting within set timelines, audit trails, protocol deviation records, and archiving of essential documents.

## Remember

- RA = link between company and regulator; strategy, dossiers, labelling, life cycle, compliance, intelligence.
- History: 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act; 1938 FD&C Act after sulfanilamide elixir (safety); 1962 Kefauver–Harris after thalidomide (efficacy); 1984 Hatch–Waxman (ANDA); 1990 ICH. India: D&C Act 1940, Rules 1945, NDCT Rules 2019.
- Non-clinical: pharmacology (including safety pharmacology core battery), ADME and toxicokinetics, toxicology (acute, repeated dose, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive).
- IND (21 CFR 312, Form 1571; investigator Form 1572): trial may start if no clinical hold within 30 days.
- IB = summary of clinical and non-clinical data for investigators; updated at least yearly.
- NDA (21 CFR 314, Form 356h); routes 505(b)(1), 505(b)(2), 505(j) ANDA.
- BE: crossover, Cmax and AUC, 90% CI within 80–125%.
- Protocol: objectives, design, subjects, treatment, assessments, safety, statistics, ethics.
- Biostatistics: α 0.05, power 80–90%, CI, t-test, ANOVA; eCTD, ICH E3, CDISC for submissions.
